highlights.title: Desk Review: Recent Methodologies on AI and Labour
highlights.summary: This toolkit synthesises recent methodologies for analysing AI's effects on employment, wages, and productivity, highlighting a critical shift from occupation-level to task-level analysis that better captures heterogeneity within jobs. The review underscores that task-based frameworks reveal more nuanced displacement dynamics than traditional occupational classifications. (Papagiannaki & Geisler, Zenodo, 2026-03-06)

highlights.title: Enhancing BLS Methodologies for Projecting AI's Impact on Employment
highlights.summary: This policy paper proposes comprehensive enhancements to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics forecasting methods, arguing that traditional extrapolation techniques are inadequate for capturing AI-driven labor market transformation. The authors present a data-driven framework for measuring occupational exposure and displacement risk across sectors. (Joshi, Preprints, 2026-03-06)

highlights.title: AI and the Future of Work: Occupational Status Perceptions Among University Students
highlights.summary: A survey of university students finds that AI is reshaping perceptions of occupational social status, with students re-evaluating the prestige and long-term viability of various careers in light of automation risk. The study highlights that entry-level and routine white-collar roles are perceived as most vulnerable, influencing students' career alignment decisions. (Liu et al., Behavioral Sciences, 2026-03-04)

highlights.title: Digital Technology Facilitates Union Busting: Surveillance and Worker Suppression
highlights.summary: This study documents how employers leverage digital technologies—including AI-powered surveillance and automated scheduling—to counter union organizing efforts, erecting new barriers to collective bargaining in the United States. The findings suggest algorithmic management tools are increasingly deployed as instruments of labor control, with downstream effects on worker wages and conditions. (Reiber et al., arXiv, 2026-03-03)

highlights.title: Capability Thresholds in Embodied Intelligence Trigger Phase Transitions in Manufacturing Geography
highlights.summary: This paper argues that advances in embodied AI and robotics represent a paradigm-level disruption to manufacturing topology not seen since Ford's assembly line, with capability thresholds triggering abrupt geographic and structural shifts in production. The analysis implies significant displacement of manufacturing-adjacent white-collar and operational roles as intelligent automation matures. (Fang, Tao & Li, arXiv, 2026-03-03)

themes: Task-level analysis is supplanting occupation-level frameworks as the preferred methodology for measuring AI-driven labor market disruption
Employers are deploying AI and digital surveillance tools not only to automate work but also to suppress collective worker action, compressing wage bargaining power
Entry-level and routine white-collar workers face heightened perceived displacement risk, shaping career decisions among the next generation of labor market entrants
Embodied AI and robotics are approaching capability thresholds that could trigger non-linear, geography-reshaping disruptions to manufacturing and adjacent sectors
Policy institutions such as the BLS are under pressure to modernize labor forecasting methodologies to adequately capture the pace and breadth of AI-driven transformation

watching.title: DARE Framework: Global Model for Responsible AI Deployment
watching.reason: Proposes governance responses to AI-driven labor polarization and inequality; signals growing regulatory momentum that could reshape adoption rates and displacement trajectories.

watching.title: Automated Machines, Robotics and Employment in Nigeria
watching.reason: Early evidence from emerging-market banking and retail sectors on automation displacement; useful for benchmarking global vs. US displacement patterns.

watching.title: daVinci-Env: Open SWE Environment Synthesis at Scale
watching.reason: Scaling of autonomous software engineering agents could accelerate tech-sector displacement; worth monitoring for downstream labor-market signals.
